What are function operations?

Functions can be combined like numbers: added, subtracted, multiplied and divided. They can also be composed, feeding the output of one into the other: (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)). An inverse function f−1 undoes f: if f(2)=7, then f−1(7)=2.

Try changing the input

Swap f and g. For f(x)=2x+3 and g(x)=x2−1, f(g(x))=2x2+1 but g(f(x))=4x2+12x+8: composition is not commutative.

What this calculator does

  • Combine: for any two functions, gives f∘g, g∘f, f+g, f−g, f⋅g and f/g, simplified. With a value x0 it also evaluates them, inside out.
  • Inverse: for ax+bcx+d, a(x−h)n+k and a⋅bx+k, finds f−1, the domain and range of both, and checks that f(f−1(x))=x.

The ideas behind it

Composition is a pipeline. In f(g(x)), g acts first and f acts on its output. The domain of f∘g contains only the inputs that g accepts and whose outputs f accepts.

An inverse swaps inputs and outputs. Every point (a,b) on the graph of f becomes (b,a) on the graph of f−1, so the two graphs are mirror images in the line y=x. The domain of f−1 is the range of f, and the other way round.

Only one-to-one functions have inverses

If two inputs give the same output, the inverse would not know which one to return. x2 is not one-to-one, but it is on the restricted domain x≥0, whose inverse is x.

Variables explained

SymbolMeaning
f,gThe two functions.
f∘g"f of g": apply g, then f.
f−1The inverse of f. It is not 1f.

Domain, rangeThe allowed inputs and the possible outputs.

How to find an inverse

  1. Write y=f(x).
  2. Swap x and y.
  3. Solve for y. The result is f−1(x).

For y=ax+bcx+d: swapping gives x(cy+d)=ay+b. Collecting the y-terms, y(cx−a)=b−dx, so

f−1(x)=−dx+bcx−a.

This works only when ad−bc≠0; otherwise f is a constant.

Complete worked example

Problem

For f(x)=2x+3 and g(x)=x2−1, find f(g(x)), g(f(x)) and both at x=2.

Step 1: f(g(x))

f(g(x))=2(x2−1)+3=2x2+1

Step 2: g(f(x))

g(f(x))=(2x+3)2−1=4x2+12x+8

Step 3: At x = 2, inside out

g(2)=3⇒f(3)=9,f(2)=7⇒g(7)=48

Check

2(2)2+1=9 and 4(4)+24+8=48. ✓

Second worked example: an inverse

Problem

Find the inverse of f(x)=2x+1x−3, with its domain and range.

Step 1: Swap and solve

x=2y+1y−3  ⇒  xy−3x=2y+1  ⇒  y(x−2)=3x+1 f−1(x)=3x+1x−2

Step 2: Domain and range

f is undefined at x=3 and never reaches y=2. So f has domain x≠3 and range y≠2, and f−1 has domain x≠2 and range y≠3.

Check

f(4)=91=9, and f−1(9)=287=4. ✓

Practical applications

  • Unit conversions: converting °C to °F and back are inverse functions; chaining conversions is composition.
  • Engineering models: sensor output as a function of temperature, and the inverse to read temperature from the output.
  • Finance: compound growth A=P(1+r)t and its inverse, the logarithm, give the time to reach a target.
  • Signal processing: a chain of filters is a composition of functions.

Common mistakes

  1. Composing in the wrong order. f(g(x)) applies g first.
  2. Treating f−1 as a reciprocal. f−1(x)≠1f(x).
  3. Missing brackets when substituting. f(g(x)) for f(x)=x2 is (x+1)2, not x2+1.
  4. Forgetting to restrict the domain. x2 needs x≥0 before it has an inverse.

Assumptions and limitations

  • In combine mode, f and g may use powers, fractions, roots and functions such as exp, ln and sin. Polynomial and rational results are expanded and reduced.
  • Inverse mode covers three families of functions; the square power uses the domain x≥h.
  • The domain of a composition is described in words; it is not computed for every expression.

Frequently asked questions

How do I find f(g(x))?

Replace every x in f with the whole expression g(x), in brackets, and simplify.

How do I find an inverse function?

Write y = f(x), swap x and y, and solve for y.

How are the graphs of f and f⁻¹ related?

They are reflections of each other in the line y = x.

Is f(g(x)) the same as g(f(x))?

Usually not. They are equal only for special pairs, such as a function and its inverse.
